content: A life cycle refers to the period encompassing one generation of an organism, achieved through either asexual or sexual reproduction. Based on ploidy, there are three distinct types of life cycles: haplontic, diplontic, and diplobiontic (also known as diplohaplontic, haplodiplontic, or dibiontic life cycles). These cycles involve alternating haploid and diploid stages. To transition back to the haploid stage, meiosis must occur. The differences between these cycles lie in the product of meiosis and whether mitosis (growth) occurs. In zygotic and gametic meiosis, there is only one mitotic stage. In zygotic meiosis, mitosis occurs during the haploid (n) phase, while in gametic meiosis, it occurs during the diploid (2n) phase. Collectively, these are termed haplobiontic cycles, as there is a single mitotic phase. In contrast, sporic meiosis involves two mitotic events, one in each phase, and is therefore classified as diplobiontic. Haplotonic Life Cycle Zygotic meiosis occurs immediately after karyogamy, the fusion of two cell nuclei. This process ends the diploid phase of the organism and produces several haploid cells. These haploid cells undergo mitotic division to form either larger, multicellular individuals or additional haploid cells. Gametes (male and female) from these individuals or cells fuse to form a zygote. In this cycle, the zygote is the only diploid cell, and mitosis occurs exclusively in the haploid phase. The resulting individuals or cells are haplonts, hence the term haplontic life cycle. Examples of haplonts include most fungi, some green algae, and many protozoa. Diplontic Life Cycle In gametic meiosis, the zygote does not immediately undergo meiosis to produce haploid cells. Instead, it divides mitotically to form a multicellular diploid individual or a group of unicellular diploid cells. Cells from these diploid individuals then undergo meiosis to produce haploid cells or gametes. While haploid cells may divide to form more haploid cells (as seen in some yeasts), the haploid phase is not the dominant phase of the life cycle. Gametes typically form quickly and fuse to produce diploid zygotes. In this cycle, gametes are usually the only haploid cells, and mitosis occurs predominantly in the diploid phase. The multicellular diploid individual is referred to as a diplont, and this life cycle is also called a diplontic life cycle. An example of this is brewer's yeast. Life History The term life history is considered more appropriate than life cycle in certain contexts, such as for red algae (Rhodophyta). In Rhodophyceae, there are generally three stages, making the term alternation of generations unsuitable. Life History Theory In the context of animal and human biology, life history theory is a framework for understanding evolved behaviors and strategies aimed at optimizing reproductive success.
